newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Albright tells Russia Baltics can join NATO.
newsitem.headline: Albright tells Russia Baltics can join NATO.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told Russians firmly on Sunday that the Baltic states were eligible to join NATO despite Moscow's fierce opposition to former Soviet republics gaining entry.

"We have said all along that NATO is open to all democratic market systems in Europe," Albright said when asked in a Russian television interview whether Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia could become NATO members.
"All those kind of countries are eligible. It doesn't matter where a country is on the map, they are eligible for membership in NATO," she said.

Albright, who arrived in Russia's second city on Saturday as part of a swing through Eastern Europe to explain NATO's expansion policy, was due to meet Baltic foreign ministers later on Sunday in the Lithuanian capital Vilnius.

She was expected to assure them that they were not excluded from membership in the alliance even though a NATO summit in Madrid last week neither invited them to join nor identified them as candidates for the next round of enlargement.
The summit invited Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to begin accession talks to become the first new NATO members since the Cold War ended at the close of the 1980s.

The Baltic states were incorporated into the Soviet Union during World War Two and became independent in 1991. Still fearful for their freedom, the three countries are anxious to gain the protection of NATO membership as soon as possible.

But Russia, which has grudgingly accepted the expansion of the alliance into Central Europe, has said it may tear up a recently signed charter of cooperation with NATO if former Soviet republics are admitted to the alliance.
Despite the differences over NATO, Albright said she had a "wonderful" meeting on Saturday evening with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on arms control and other issues.

U.S. officials said a major theme of the talks was how to adapt the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty to the changed political situation. Albright held another meeting with Primakov directly after the television interview.
Albright said U.S.-Russian relations with Russia were "on a very strong basis".

U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin were "working very hard to show that there is a new Russia that works with the United States together for peace and security", she said.
Asked about economic relations, she called on Russia to ensure that its commercial and tax laws were favourable to American investment.

Albright, who was born in the former Czechoslovakia and speaks several languages, made a brief opening statement in Russian noting that Saturday's meeting was her eighth with Primakov. She also corrected an omission by her interpreter at one point in the interview.
